## Section 1A: Improving R Code 

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  a = 1:10,
  b = seq(200, 400, length=10),
  c = 11:20,
  d = NA
)

df
```

```{r}
df$a <- (df$a - min(df$a)) / (max(df$a) - min(df$a))

df$b <- (df$b - min(df$a)) / (max(df$b) - min(df$b))

df$c <- (df$c - min(df$c)) / (max(df$c) - min(df$c))

df$d <- (df$d - min(df$d)) / (max(df$a) - min(df$d))
```


> To work with original values, data frame is reset 

```{r}
normalize <- function(x) {

  if (all(is.na(x))) {
  return(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))
  }
  
  # Find the minimum and maximum, ignoring missing values
  min_value <- min(x, na.rm=TRUE)
  max_value <- max(x, na.rm=TRUE)

  # Return missing values if normalization is not possible
  if (!is.finite(min_value) || !is.finite(max_value) ||
      min_value == max_value) {
    return(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))
  }

  # Normalize values between 0 and 1
  result <- (x - min_value) / (max_value - min_value)

  return(result)
}
```


> Test run of funtion: 

```{r}
normalize(c(2, 4, 6))
```

```{r}
df_normalized <- as.data.frame(lapply(df, normalize))

df_normalized
```

> I created a normalization function to avoid repeating the same calculations for each column. The function scales numerical values between 0 and 1 and handles missing values. This makes the code easier to use and read. 


## Section 1B: Protein Structure Analysis 

```{r}
library(bio3d)
```


```{r}

s1 <- read.pdb("4AKE")
s2 <- read.pdb("1AKE")
s3 <- read.pdb("1E4Y")
```

```{r}
s1.chainA <- trim.pdb(s1, chain="A", elety="CA")
s2.chainA <- trim.pdb(s2, chain="A", elety="CA")
s3.chainA <- trim.pdb(s3, chain="A", elety="CA")
```


```{r}
s1.b <- s1.chainA$atom$b
s2.b <- s2.chainA$atom$b
s3.b <- s3.chainA$atom$b
```



```{r}
plotb3(s1.b, sse=s1.chainA, typ="l", ylab="Bfactor")
```

## Questions 1-5

> **Q1.** What type of object is returned from `read.pdb()`?

- The `read.pdb()`function returns a PDB object that has information about a protein structure like atomic coordinates. 

> **Q2.** What does `trim.pdb()` do?

- The `trim.pdb()` function selects specific parts of a protein structure. 

> **Q3.** What input parameter would turn off the marginal black and gray rectangles, and what do they represent?

- The `sse=NULL` input removes the black and gray rectangles representing secondary-structure regions. 

>**Q4.** What would be a better plot to compare across the different proteins?

- An overlapping line plot because the B-factor values would be displayed on the same graph. 

>**Q5.** Which proteins are more similar in their B-factor trends, and how could you quantify this?

```{r}
length(s1.b)
length(s2.b)
length(s3.b)
```

Since all three vectors have the same length we will use the following: 

```{r}
hc <- hclust(dist(rbind(s1.b, s2.b, s3.b)))

plot(hc)
```

- The proteins 1AKE and 1E4Y have most similar B-factor trends because they cluster together at a lower height in the graph. Their similarity can be quantified using `dist()` to calculate distances and `hclust()` to group proteins based on their B-factor values. 

## Q6: How would you generalize the original code above to work with any set of input protein structures?

```{r}

library(bio3d)

# Function 1: Analyze one protein
# Input: A PDB ID and an optional chain ID.
# Purpose: Read a protein structure and plot its B-factors.
# Usage: plot_protein("4AKE")
# Output: A B-factor plot for one protein.

plot_protein <- function(pdb_id, chain = "A") {

  # Read the protein structure
  protein <- read.pdb(pdb_id)

  # Select the chosen chain and alpha-carbon atoms
  protein_chain <- trim.pdb(protein, chain = chain, elety = "CA")

  # Extract B-factor values
  b_values <- protein_chain$atom$b

  # Create a B-factor plot
  plotb3(b_values, sse = protein_chain,
         typ = "l", ylab = "Bfactor")
}

# Function 2: Analyze multiple proteins
# Input: A vector of PDB IDs and an optional chain ID.
# Purpose: Generate plots for multiple protein structures.
# Usage: plot_proteins(c("4AKE", "1AKE", "1E4Y"))
# Output: A separate B-factor plot for each protein.

plot_proteins <- function(pdb_ids, chain = "A") {

  # Repeat the analysis for each PDB ID
  for (id in pdb_ids) {

    # Call the original function
    plot_protein(id, chain = chain)
  }
}


```

Test function: 

```{r}
plot_protein("4AKE")
plot_protein("1AKE")
plot_protein("1E4Y")
```

> My function accepts a PDB ID. The `read.pdb()`function is used to retrieve a protein structure and `trim.pdb()` to select alpha-carbon atoms. Then, it extracts the B-factor values and creates a plot. This allows multiple proteins to be analyzed without repeating the same code.
